text_to_speech: okay here's the gun I'm trying to measure the muzzle velocity of brake Barrel um takes 22 caliber pellet and here's the setup I basically constructed a pendulum that hangs in front of this protractor here and at the end of the pendulum is a ball of clay what I can do is fire the gun Point Blank into the ball of clay that causes it to swing and then I can measure The Arc Length of That Swing because I know how long the pendulum string is and I know the mass of the ball and I can approximate the mass of these pellets but I don't have a very good scale and basically um the pellet from this gun doesn't wedge very far into the clay it goes maybe half a centimeter into the clay so it's a pretty inelastic collision and um and um thanks to conservation of momentum I can know the momentum of the the ball after the collision and so I can determine the approximate velocity of the um pellet coming out of the gun but it's very simple just a couple pieces of wood and a protractor that I printed off the internet in a ball of clay

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Okay, here's the gun I'm trying to measure the muzzle velocity of. It's a brake barrel.
It takes 22 caliber pellet.
And here's the setup.
I basically constructed a pendulum that hangs in front of this protractor here.
And the end of the pendulum is a ball of clay.
And what I can do is fire the gun point blank into the ball of clay.
And it causes it to swing.
And then I can measure the arc length of that swing.
Because I know how long the pendulum string is.
And I know the mass of the ball.
And I can approximate the mass of these pellets, but I don't have a very good scale.
And basically the pellet from this gun doesn't wedge very far into the clay.
It goes maybe half a centimeter into the clay.
So it's a pretty inelastic collision.
And thanks to the conservation of momentum, I can know the momentum of the ball after the collision.
And so I can determine the approximate velocity of the pellet coming out of the gun.
But it's very simple.
There's a couple pieces of wood.
And a protractor that I printed off the internet.
And a ball of clay.

youtube_description: Experimental setup to measure the muzzle velocity of my pellet gun using the following household items: Wood planks and some nails (to mount everything), 125 grams modeling clay, several feet of 6 lb. fishing line, 1 fishing weight (an egg sinker at the core of the clay ball), protractor printed on a piece of paper, a video camera, a tape measure, and a scale. You'll have to look up the physics on your own :) Oh, and you can't really see the fishing line swinging in front of the protractor in this video, but you could in the original.
youtube_title: Measuring the muzzle velocity of .22 caliber spring-piston pellet pistol
